title: Performance Management, Career and Succession Planning — Organisational Process Flow
subtitle: Planning · monitoring · review · calibration · reward · talent and succession · early remediation · LRA ss.186(2)(a), 187, 188, 191, 192 · Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294) items 14–20 · EEA ss.5, 6(4), 11, 15, 20 · Skills Development Act and SETA Grant Regulations · BCEA · POPIA ss.11, 23, 26, 71 · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells an organisation what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment the strategic plan is approved until the year's ratings have been calibrated, rewarded and turned into development, talent and succession decisions, and the results feed back into the next cycle. It covers the full domain that the GBS Process Architecture assigns to Performance Management, Career and Succession Planning: job profiles, gap analysis, KPA and KPI design and weighting, the gap to the next position, and the 9-box. It is built from the End-to-End Performance Management Process supplied for this flow (1 October 2026), corrected and supplemented as recorded in section 15.

notes.text: Every employee moves through one annual spine (plan, contract, monitor, assess, reward and develop, govern) with continuous check-ins underneath. The same evidence then drives one of two paths:
points: Grow — the default for everyone meeting or exceeding standard: recognition, reward, development, talent pools, succession slates and career moves (Phase 5).

Remediate — for a sustained gap against a known standard: early warning, a diagnostic screen, informal counselling and, where the cause is capacity, a hand-off to the GBS Incapacity flow (Track 2A) for the performance improvement plan (PIP). Wilful underperformance goes to the GBS Misconduct flow; a health or disability cause goes to Incapacity Track 2B; a systemic cause is fixed by management, not the employee.

notes.text: The flow applies to permanent and fixed-term employees, including managers and executives. Probationers follow the same planning and check-in steps with the probation rules in step 2.7. Workers placed by a temporary employment service (TES) are employed by the TES, which runs any formal process while the client supplies performance input under the TES agreement, unless they earn below the BCEA earnings threshold and have been placed for more than 3 months other than as a temporary service: the client is then their sole employer and they enter this flow directly (LRA s.198A(3)(b); step 0.15). The flow assumes no collective agreement or bargaining council agreement regulates performance management, merit pay or bonuses; where one does, it prevails and this flow must be adjusted.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: No statute prescribes how an employer must manage performance. Setting standards, measuring work and rewarding results are part of the employer's right to direct and control work, exercised within the contract of employment and four bodies of law. (1) The LRA: a dismissal for poor work performance must be for a fair reason and follow a fair procedure (ss.188, 192), and unfair conduct relating to promotion, demotion, probation, training or the provision of benefits is an unfair labour practice (s.186(2)(a)). (2) The Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 ("the Code"), issued under s.203 and in effect from 4 September 2025, which repealed the Schedule 8 Code of Good Practice: Dismissal. Items 14 to 18 govern probation and items 19 and 20 govern poor work performance after probation; anyone deciding the fairness of a dismissal must take the Code into account (s.188(2), s.203(3)). (3) The EEA: every employer must eliminate unfair discrimination in any employment policy or practice, which includes performance evaluation and remuneration (ss.1, 5, 6(1)); a difference in terms and conditions between employees doing the same or substantially the same work, or work of equal value, that is directly or indirectly based on a listed ground is unfair discrimination (s.6(4)); where a listed ground is alleged the employer must prove the difference is fair (s.11(1)), while for an arbitrary ground the complainant carries that burden (s.11(2)). (4) POPIA: performance records are personal information, and some of what check-ins surface (health, disability) is special personal information. The Skills Development Act and the SETA Grant Regulations add an annual reporting duty that the development plans in this flow feed (Workplace Skills Plan and Annual Training Report, due 30 April each year). A review on 19 October 2026 found no amendment to the Code since publication. The Labour Law Amendment Bill, 2025 (published for comment on 26 February 2026) is DRAFT only and not law; it is tracked at step 6.7. Status should be re-checked before adoption.

notes.heading: Figures in force today
notes.text: BCEA earnings threshold: R269,600.90 a year from 1 May 2026; it decides who may take an EEA s.10 dispute to CCMA arbitration and who is protected by LRA ss.198A–198B (relevant to TES workers' bonus eligibility). WSP/ATR deadline: 30 April each year (2027 cycle: 30 April 2027); late submission forfeits the mandatory grant of 20% of skills development levies paid (SETA Grant Regulations reg 4(4)), unless the SETA has granted an extension of up to one month on written request (reg 4(8)).

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: LAW = a statute or regulation in force (LRA, BCEA, EEA and Regulations, POPIA, PAIA, Skills Development Act and Levies Act, SETA Grant Regulations, Income Tax Act); binding now.

Code = a code of good practice: the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (cited by item number), the Code of Good Practice on Equal Pay / Remuneration for Work of Equal Value (GN 448, 2015), the Code on the Employment of Persons with Disabilities (GN 1085, GG 39383, 2015) and the Code of Good Practice on the Prevention and Elimination of Harassment in the Workplace (GN R.1890, GG 46056, 2022). Must be taken into account; departures must be justified.
CL = a principle from case law, cited by name, court and year. Verify the citation and any later authority before using it in advice.

BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt as policy so it becomes binding internally. All weights, scales, frequencies and periods marked BP are recommendations to be calibrated to each client.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: The performance record is the incapacity record. If an employee is ever dismissed for poor work performance, the employer will have to show that the employee failed to meet a standard; that the employee knew or could reasonably be expected to know it; was given a fair opportunity to meet it; that it was reasonably achievable; and that dismissal was appropriate (item 20(1)). It will also have to show appropriate evaluation, instruction, training, guidance or counselling and a reasonable period to improve (item 19(1)), and that the employee was given an opportunity to respond (item 19(2)). This flow is built so that every one of those facts is proved by a document made at the time in the ordinary course of the cycle — the signed agreement (known standard), the calibration record (reasonable and consistent standard), the check-in notes and PDP (evaluation, guidance and support), the mid-year gap confirmation (fair warning) — long before anyone opens an incapacity file. The same records defend reward and promotion decisions against unfair labour practice and equal-pay claims, because a pay difference based on performance is defensible only if the evaluation system is applied equally to everyone it covers.

notes.heading: Ten interpretation points that shape the flow
points: Prerogative, but not unilateral change. The employer may set reasonable standards without the employee's agreement (step 2.4). But introducing a performance system that changes how pay, increases or bonuses are earned may change terms and conditions of employment: consult, and where contractual entitlements change, agree or follow a lawful process (LRA s.64(4); step 0.2). Where a workplace forum exists, criteria for merit increases or discretionary bonuses are a matter for consultation (LRA s.84(1)(h); education and training are also a consultation matter under s.84(1)(i)).

Can't or won't, then which flow. Poor performance because the employee cannot do the work is incapacity (items 19–20). Poor performance because the employee will not do it is misconduct. A health or disability cause is ill-health incapacity (item 21) and engages the EEA. A cause in the system (unclear standard, missing tools, impossible workload) is not the employee's problem at all. The diagnostic router (step R2) chooses one route and records why; if facts change, switch routes openly. Poor performance is never dealt with under the disciplinary code, and PIP records are not disciplinary records.

A rating is not, by itself, a dispute the CCMA can hear. Section 186(2)(a) covers promotion, demotion, probation, training and benefits, not ratings as such. A rating becomes justiciable when it decides a benefit (a merit increase or bonus), a promotion, training or a demotion, or when it is alleged to be discriminatory (EEA s.6). That is why the internal objection route (section 10) must be real: it is the only forum for most rating disagreements. Whether a discretionary bonus is a "benefit" depends on the scheme; the Labour Appeal Court has held that a benefit includes an advantage granted under a policy or practice subject to the employer's discretion (CL: Apollo Tyres SA v CCMA, DA1/11, LAC, 21 February 2013).

Equal application. Performance is a recognised ground for paying people differently for equal work, but only where the evaluation system is applied equally (EE Regulations, 2025 (GN 6125) reg 7(1)(c) and 7(2): employees must be equally subject to a consistently applied evaluation system, and the difference must not be biased against a listed group and must be applied proportionately; Code on Equal Pay, GN 448, 2015). Calibration (Phase 4), the equal-pay check (step 5.3) and the adverse-impact review (step 6.2) exist to prove it.

A changed standard is a new standard. It must be communicated, dated and given a reasonable lead-in before it is assessed (item 20(1)(b)(i)–(ii)). Mid-cycle resets (step 3.6) are recorded as dated amendments.

Statutory leave is neutral. An employee may not be rated down, or lose a bonus pro rata beyond the scheme's stated rules, because of maternity, parental, adoption, commissioning-parental, sick or COIDA leave. Rate the period actually worked (step 4.9). Penalising pregnancy-related absence risks an automatically unfair dismissal or discrimination claim (LRA s.187(1)(e); BCEA ss.25–25C; EEA s.6(1)). Since Van Wyk v Minister of Employment and Labour (CC, 3 October 2025), BCEA ss.25–25C are read so that two employed parents may share 4 months and 10 days of parental leave; rate neutrally whichever parent takes it.

Disability and accommodation. Where a gap is linked to a disability, the question becomes reasonable accommodation, not a PIP (EEA s.1, definition of reasonable accommodation, and s.6; Disability Code, GN 1085, GG 39383, 2015). Targets for an accommodated employee may be adjusted; the adjustment is recorded, not hidden.

Senior employees and probationers. For managers and senior or highly skilled employees, a formal PIP and a warning may not be required where they can judge their own performance or a lapse would have severe consequences (item 20(2)); they must still be told and allowed to respond (item 19(2)). Stating that expectation in the agreement (step 2.8) makes it easier to rely on later. Probation now tests suitability as well as performance, and the employee must be heard before probation is extended or the appointment not confirmed (items 14–18).

A human decides. No rating, reward, PIP or talent placement may be based solely on automated processing that profiles the employee (POPIA s.71). AI summaries and analytics may support managers, but a named person decides and can explain why. This goes beyond the s.71 minimum (s.71(2)–(3) permit exceptions with safeguards, such as a chance to make representations and information about the underlying logic) and is adopted as BP; each tool is governed under the GBS POPIA and AI Compliance flows.

Counting time. Internal steps use working days (BP). Statutory referral periods are calendar days: exclude the first day and include the last; if the last day is a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday, it moves to the next working day (CCMA Rules, rule 3; Interpretation Act 33 of 1957 s.4 for other periods). The cycle is expressed in months relative to the financial year: Month 0 is the month before the year starts; Month 12 is its last month.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: HR Business Partner (HRBP, the process owner and spine; in smaller organisations the HR manager); Line Manager (LM); Next-level Manager (NLM); Employee (EMP); Executive Committee (EXCO); Board and Remuneration Committee (REMCO); Calibration Panel (CAL, divisional head, peer managers and an HR facilitator); Talent Committee (TC); Learning and Development (L&D); Skills Development Facilitator (SDF) and Training Committee (TCOM); Employment Equity Manager (EEM, the senior manager assigned under EEA s.24); Employee Relations Officer (ERO, case owner in the Incapacity and Misconduct flows); Payroll (PAY); Information Officer (IO); HRIS owner (IT); Legal Adviser (LA). The employee's representative (REP: a co-employee or trade union representative); stakeholder and 360-degree raters (RAT); coach or mentor (MEN). External: SETA; TES provider (TES); Employee Assistance Programme (EAP); trade union or workplace forum (TU); CCMA or bargaining council (CCMA/BC); Labour Court (LC); Information Regulator (IR).

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger. It must be in place before the first agreement is signed, because whether a standard was known and reasonable, whether a pay difference is justified, and whether performance data may lawfully be processed are all decided by documents that must already exist.

notes.heading: Employee side of Phase 0
notes.text: Employees owe nothing yet, but their later rights depend on this phase. An employee rated against a profile that was never shared, or denied a bonus under rules never communicated, has a strong objection and possibly an unfair labour practice claim.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: A policy that says ratings are "calibrated to a curve" invites the argument that ratings were lowered to fit a quota rather than measured against the agreed standard. Use the distribution as a diagnostic lens only (step 4.4).

stages.title: Remediation branch R — from early warning to the Incapacity flow
intro: Check-in agenda (15–30 minutes). (1) What has progressed since we last met — evidence against key results? (2) What is in the way, and what support do you need? (3) Feedback both ways: what is working, what to adjust. (4) Are priorities still right, or do key results need to change? (5) Development: what did you learn, what is next? (6) Agreed actions, owners and dates.

Coaching stance. Managers lead as well as manage. The GROW model (Goal, Reality, Options, Way forward) structures the conversation. In transactional-analysis terms, the manager speaks from the Adult ego state, balancing high connection (nurturing) with high task clarity, so that the relationship lands in the high-performance quadrant rather than comfort, apathy or fear. Smart trust is extended on evidence of character and competence and adjusted as evidence changes.

Branch R is the bridge between ordinary management and a formal incapacity process. It is short, developmental and documented. It does not duplicate the Incapacity flow: once a capacity cause is confirmed and informal steps have not worked, the PIP runs under Incapacity Track 2A (steps 2A.1–2A.10, forms I06–I09), and this flow keeps running alongside it.

notes.heading: Watch

rows: Guiding principles and section 15: development "as Schedule 8 of the LRA requires"; leader training on "Schedule 8 compliance"
Schedule 8 was repealed on 4 September 2025. Cite the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294), items 19–20 (poor work performance) and 14–18 (probation).

Wrong items even under the repealed Code: old items 8–9 dealt with poor work performance; items 10–11 dealt with ill health. Replace with Code items 19–20, and item 21 only where the cause is ill health.
Section 2: consider whether the employee knew the standard, whether it was reasonable, and alternatives

Incomplete against item 20(1). Add: whether the employee was given a fair opportunity to meet the standard, and whether dismissal was an appropriate sanction; and item 19(2), the opportunity to respond before dismissal.
Section 1.5 and 5: "A changed standard … reasonable lead-in (Schedule 8)"
Keep the rule; cite item 20(1)(b)(i)–(ii) and add a BP minimum lead-in (step 1.7).
Section 12.2 step 2: informal counselling is an "off-the-record discussion"
An unrecorded conversation cannot later prove that the employee knew of the concern. Keep it informal and non-disciplinary, but keep a short, shared note (PM26).
Section 12.2: PIP templates T1–T7 and 6–12 week PIP

Avoid a second PIP template set. Use the Incapacity flow's forms: T1 → PM26 / I06; T2 → I06 (add a notice-to-attend section); T3 → I07; T4 → I08 interim review; T5 successful → I08 final review; T6 extended → I08 with extension reasons; T7 unsuccessful → I08 final review and I24 decision memo. The PIP period follows Incapacity step 2A.5 (BP 30–90 days); v1.1 replaced the earlier 6–12 week figure (see R5).

Cite items 14–18: probation now assesses suitability as well as performance; reasonable guidance and counselling (item 17); representations before extension or non-confirmation (item 18(1)); probation not to be used to deprive employees of permanent status (item 15(2)). Route through Incapacity step 2A.10.
Section 12.5: shorter process for senior and specialist employees because they can self-assess

Item 20(2) also covers a highly skilled employee where a departure from a high standard would have severe consequences; in both cases item 19(2) still requires an opportunity to respond. Record the justification (Incapacity 2A.9).
Section 9 table: rating 1 → "PIP (section 12) if not already in place"
A PIP should never start because of a year-end rating: by then the concern must already have been confirmed at mid-year (step 3.7). A PIP also follows diagnosis (R2), not the rating alone.
Complete band table and rounding rule added (section 7), with a compliance-gate cap.
Section 13: disputes about an unfair labour practice "(for example promotion or benefits)"

A rating is not by itself an unfair labour practice. Add demotion, training and probation (s.186(2)(a)); state the 90-day ULP, 30-day dismissal and 6-month EEA referral periods; note the uncertainty over discretionary bonuses as "benefits" (CL: Apollo Tyres, DA1/11, LAC 2013: a benefit can include an advantage granted under a discretionary policy or practice).

Correct, but add the reason it matters: performance justifies a pay difference only under an evaluation system that is equally applied (EE Regulations, 2025 (GN 6125) reg 7(1)(c), 7(2): employees equally subject to a consistently applied system, and the difference applied proportionately; Code on Equal Pay, GN 448, 2015). Calibration and the adverse-impact review prove equal application.
Section 10: withholding a discretionary bonus follows scheme rules communicated in advance
Keep; add that clawback or recovery by deduction needs a lawful basis (BCEA s.34) and that Remco discretion must be exercised rationally and recorded.
Section 11: placements confidential; employees receive "the development outcome, not a box label"

Confidential is not the same as undisclosable. A 9-box placement is the employee's personal information and may be requested under POPIA s.23 or PAIA; write placements and potential notes on that basis (step 5.13).
Section 14: records kept for "the longer of the statutory retention period or the life of any dispute"

There is no single statutory period for performance records. Set a schedule (step 0.9): life of employment plus 3 years (BP); BCEA s.31 3 years for remuneration records; incapacity and dispute files until finally determined.
Wellbeing responses may reveal health information (special personal information, POPIA s.26). Require anonymity, a minimum aggregation group and no use in ratings (step 0.8).
Section 2: collective and recognition agreements cover "representation rights and any agreed performance or bonus rules"

Add the duty to consult before introducing or changing a pay-linked system, the risk of a unilateral change to terms (LRA s.64(4)), and workplace-forum consultation on merit-increase and bonus criteria (LRA s.84(1)(h)).
Added step 4.9 and interpretation point 6: rate the period worked; never rate down for maternity, parental, sick or COIDA leave (LRA s.187(1)(e); BCEA ss.25–25C; EEA s.6).
Added the WSP/ATR link (steps 0.10, 5.14, 6.4): PDP learning feeds the WSP; delivered training feeds the ATR; submission by 30 April each year.
Silent on TES workers and on harassment risk
Added step 0.15 and 2.9 (TES as employer; from v1.1, the client as sole employer of deemed employees) and P8 (performance management used as bullying, Harassment Code, GN R.1890, 2022).
Domain scope: career and succession treated briefly

Added job profiles, gap analysis and the gap to the next position (steps 0.4, 1.3, 5.10) to match the GBS Architecture definition of the domain, and linked succession to the Resourcing flow's path (c).

intro: Resourcing flow. It refers to "the GBS Performance Management, Career and Succession process" for job profiles and the succession register (its steps 0.5–0.6). In this flow these are PM04 (step 0.4) and PM35 (step 5.11). Resourcing v2.0 form RS09 (succession / talent register extract, used at step 1.4 and for path (c)) is an extract of PM35; the "Succession flow (planned)" source shown for RS09 is this flow. Its probation reviews at day 30, 60 and 90 (step 5.10) and the RS40 development plan for Model 3 and succession appointees feed step 2.7 and PM20 here. Update the Resourcing cross-references to these form numbers.

Incapacity flow. I06 covers the counselling meeting record but has no notice-to-attend section for the formal PIP meeting (source T2). Add one, or add a separate form. Incapacity step 2A.3 is a formal counselling meeting; this flow's R3 is the informal step before it. The two together replace source steps 2–3.
Operational Requirements flow. Where performance is used as a selection criterion, use only calibrated ratings from this flow, and only if the criterion was agreed or is fair and objective.

The Code is silent on performance management outside dismissal. Items 19–20 test a dismissal; nothing guides ratings, PIP content or the length of the improvement period. Employers rely on case law and best practice for the whole pre-dismissal record.

Item 19(2) is thinner than the repealed item 8. The old Code required an investigation into the reasons for poor performance, consideration of alternatives and a right to be heard with a representative. The 2025 Code says only that the employee should have an opportunity to respond. This flow keeps the older safeguards as BP (R2, R3 and the Incapacity flow).

"Benefits" in s.186(2)(a). Whether a purely discretionary bonus is a benefit, and when a rating that drives it can be challenged, is not fully settled in the case law. Scheme rules should state the nature of each payment clearly.

Equal application is required but undefined. The equal-pay criteria allow performance-based differences only under an equally applied evaluation system, without saying what equal application requires. Calibration records and adverse-impact analysis are the best available evidence. The EE Regulations, 2025 (GN 6125) reg 7(1)(c) now add that the system must be consistently applied, and reg 7(2) that the differentiation must be applied proportionately and not be biased against a listed group, but they still do not define equal application.

POPIA s.71 has no guidance. Neither the Information Regulator nor a court has said when human involvement is enough to take an AI-assisted rating outside "based solely" on automated processing. The safeguards in step 0.8 are prudent, not settled.

WSP timing. The 30 April deadline and the April–March grant year do not match many employers' financial years, so PDP data for the WSP may come from a different performance cycle. Build the extract date into the calendar (step 5.14).
